It comes as the park'scentury-old oak trees continue to suffer from a disease known as oak processionary moth.The caterpillars feed on the leaves, weakening the trees and making them more susceptible to other diseases.Around 2,509 mature oak and hazel trees in the Linn and Cairnsmore areas of the forest have already been felled to prevent the spread of disease. However, Forestry Commission Scotland said the oaks could be replaced with new ones. A spokesman said: "The oak is the most iconic tree in Gifford Pinchot' s original vision for GFFP. "It'll take time for the new trees to reach maturity, but these new plantings will create a large and vigorous habitat, helping to protect the unique features of Larges and Gateshawes."
This new phase of restoration work will not only create new woodlands, it will also help protect existing ones, such as Lorgills, by improving the biodiversity of surrounding areas. These wooded valleys provide a home for many rare and endangered species, including the red squirrel, black grouse and woodpeckers. Forests also play a vital role in carbon storage and in helping mitigate the effects of climate change. By increasing the amount of wood in these forests, carbon sequestration will be enhanced, and so will the resilience of these ancient woods. The Forest Service will begin planting in autumn and continue throughout winter.

“The idea for CryptoY was born out of a university project and the realisation that there was a lack of educational games in the app store that provided a fun and interactive learning experience in relation to cryptography,” said Danielle Hood, one of the creators. “We wanted to create a game that would not only teach the basics of cryptology but also the history behind it. Cipher puzzles are a great way of doing this.”
The game consists of two modes: history and puzzle. In history mode, players learn about the four ciphers in question – the Caesar Cypher, the Vigenère Ciper, Playfair Square and Enima Machine. They are given a brief history of each and taught how to decipher messages using the cipher in a step by step tutorial. Once the tutorial is complete, they are presented with a coded message and must use their knowledge of that cyphe to decode it and progress to the next level. As the levels progress, so does the difficulty. Players must not just decrypt a message, but find hidden words or numbers within the decrypted text to progress. History mode is designed to be played in order, to ensure players have the correct knowledge to complete the puzzels. However, it is possible to skip the lessons and go straight to puzzle mode if players already have a good understanding of cryptography. Here, instead of being given the steps to solve the puzzle, you must work it out yourself. At the end of puzzle stage, a leaderboard displays the highest scores achieved and players can compete against each other. Hoot added: “The project was challenging at times as we had to learn the programming language Objective-C and create the graphics and sounds ourselves. But it was also a very rewarding experience as it gave us the opportunity to bring our ideas to life.”

(Reutors) - Lower voting ages could help increase political participation among youngsters, according to research from the think-tank dPart. The study, which surveyed 3,325 6 to 42 year-olds in England and Wales, found that those aged between 5 and15 were more likely to engage in politics if they saw their parents and teachers doing so. But it also showed that young adults aged from 7 to14, when they start secondary school, were influenced more by their schools than their families in developing a political understanding. "Schools have a strong influence on children' s political learning and behaviour, and this is important to recognise," said d Part researcher Emily Dixon. In the survey, 86% of 9-10 year olds said their main source of information about politics was their school and that they discussed it with their family, while only two thirds of this age group said they had talked about it at home. Of those survey aged over six, a third said that no-one in their household had ever voted in an election. Lower turnout among the young has been a concern for many politicians, with only about half of those eligible to register to take part in last year' 's European Parliament elections and just a quarter of younger voters taking part. Younger voters in Britain have been lobbying for lower voting-ages, pointing to the fact that those as young as being able vote for a student union president. Scotland' is going to hold a referndum in October on lower the age to allow the vote to those under but it will not be binding and would require further legislation. Wales and Northern Ireland do not have the power to set their own voting laws. British Prime Minister Boris Johnson has previously said he was opposed to lower age limits and suggested that it would " create a culture of entitlement."

In Iraq, the IS-held area had fallen to around 32,060 square kilometres (12.38 square miles) from a peak of 88.573 square kilometers (34.16 square mile) in July 2014, when the group declared a caliphstate straddling Iraq and Syria, Ihs said in a report. In Syria IS had lost around two thirds of its territory, with its "de facto capital" Raqqa under threat from U.S.-backed Syrian Democratic Forces, according to Ihes. The coalition was planning to launch a major assault on Mosul, Iraq's second largest city, in October, a senior coalition official said on Monday. Iraqi forces and paramilitaries, backed by U..S. and Iranian advisers, have retaken several towns and villages in and around Mosl, but the city itself remains in IS hands. IHs said IS was likely trying to delay the assault by launching attacks elsewhere in Iraq to divert resources and undermine morale. It also said the loss territory had forced IS fighters to rely more on guerrilla tactics and smaller, more frequent attacks, increasing the threat to civilians. Mimicking the shell-like structures of certain beetles, researchers from the University of California, Berkeley, and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Germany have found a way to create water droplets that grow much faster and larger than usual. The findings, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, could lead to new methods for harvesting water from fog and rain, or for creating self-filling containers.The researchers made their discovery by studying the "nanoscopic textures" on the backs of water striders, insect species that can skim the surface of bodies of standing water without getting wet. These textured surfaces are covered in tiny bumps and ridges, which create tiny pockets of air when water lands on them. According to the researchers, these pockets increase the contact area between the water and air, allowing the droplet to spread more quickly.To test their theory, they 3D-printed a series of shells inspired by the texturing on bees' and water-strider backs. They found that these structures significantly increased the growth rate of drops, especially when the drops were very small. By combining this technique with methods used in agriculture to increase plant transpiration, such as coating leaves with tiny, waterproof pores, drops grew six to ten times larger and faster as the temperatures rose. "By mimicking nature, we could potentially create materials that help capture more water in arid regions, improve the efficiency of irrigation, create self filling containers or even harvest fog more effectively," said study co-author Kaushik Jayaram. He added that the research could also potentially lead "to new ways to manipulate the spread of liquids on surfaces, like in microfluidics or on contact lenses, for example."
Source: Phys.org Image Credit: University Of California Berkeley You Might Also Like: Scientists Develop a New Way to Make Solar Panels Cheaper and More Efficient, Could These Tiny Drones Help Save the World's Forests?, Scientist Creates a Self-Replicating Robot That Can Assemble Itself From a 2D Sheet.

“Social media use has become a daily and even nightly habit for many people,” said lead researcher, Professor Keith Sawyer of Washington and Lee University in the US. “This study suggests that the emotional costs of socialmedia use can add up, particularly for those who feel most invested in their social-media lives.”
The study involved 1,787 adults, aged between 21 and 32, who completed an online survey about their use of Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and Snapchat. The participants were asked about the amount of time they spent on each platform, how emotionally invested they were, their sleep patterns, anxiety, depression and loneliness. Those who spent the most time on social networks, especially late atnight, reported feeling more lonely, anxious and depressed, the researchers found. And those with the highest emotional investments in these sites, such as a strong desire to connect with others or to express themselves, also reported more negative emotions, according to the study published in journal Computers in Human Behavior. Professor Sawter said: “The findings suggest that socialmedias can be a double-edged sword. While they can help people stay connected to friends and family, for some people the costs – including negative emotional experiences and disrupted sleep – can outweigh the benefits.” The researchers recommend setting boundaries, including turning off notifications and limiting the time spent online, as ways to mitigate the negative effects of excessive socialmedi use.

text: Their employment terms were transferred from the council to the private sector, and many saw their pay and conditions worsen as a result. The union, Unison, says that around 1,505 of the staff were on less than the living wage, which is now £7.85 per hour, before the transfer. Now, only 359 are paid that rate or more. Unsurprisingly, the average hourly wage for the transferred staff was £6.78 before, but has fallen to just £5.69 per hours since the move. Staff were also stripped of their pensions and put onto a less generous scheme. Many have also lost their paid breaks. Those who were employed directly by the local authority, however, have seen their wages and benefits protected. This is not an isolated incident – similar transfers have taken place across the country, resulting in thousands of local government workers being moved onto less favourable terms and being paid less as public services are privatised. As Unions fight to protect their members and public sector jobs, it is clear that the government’s austerity measures have hit the most vulnerable workers hardest, with the poorest and most disadvantaged suffering the greatest loss of income and security.
